title: The Polycrisis Apocalypse
subtitle: Global catastrophe, survivability risk, and the long-term trajectory of humanity, from unsafe stabilization to deep-time extinction
dek: A second, Global Risk & Earth Systems edition of the Polycrisis Apocalypse framework — reframed around the gap between survival and sustainable survival, and followed through centuries, millennia and deep time. Supersedes HH-2026-24.
abstract: The Polycrisis Apocalypse is a framework for thinking about a catastrophe that does not arrive as a single event. Instead of one asteroid, one war or one pandemic, it describes a long-duration unraveling in which climate instability, pollution, poverty, ecological degradation, conflict, institutional breakdown and powerful new technologies reinforce one another. The term draws on the language of the global polycrisis debate, in which several crises interact so that the whole is more dangerous than the sum of its parts.

This report examines the most pessimistic coherent version of that story. A majority of humanity is gradually pushed into survivability risk regions, meaning places and conditions where heat, toxic air, unsafe water, hunger, violence, failing health systems and fragile infrastructure threaten life or long-term wellbeing. Civilization does not vanish. It adapts just enough to continue, but it stabilizes at persistently unsafe levels, or it worsens, across centuries, millennia and potentially tens or hundreds of thousands of years. In the terminal scenario, the accumulated damage and a final existential shock end the human story.

The central thesis is that the defining feature of the Polycrisis Apocalypse is the gap between survival and sustainable survival. Humanity can persist, even prosper in places, while the underlying crisis is never resolved and the margin for survival narrows. The report builds the mechanism across definition, convergence, the risk envelope, regional expansion, the geography of exposure, stabilization and feedback, then follows the trajectory through centuries, millennia and deep time to the terminal pathways, before turning to scenario architecture, counterarguments, early-warning indicators and what would break the trajectory.

The framework is explicitly a hypothetical structure rather than a forecast. Long instability does not imply certain extinction: extinction tens or hundreds of thousands of years out is a terminal scenario offered for analysis, not a prediction. The framework’s value lies in showing how a civilization can remain vulnerable long after the initial catastrophe has passed.
findings: The baseline is already severe: roughly 2.3 billion people face moderate or severe food insecurity, about 2.2 billion lack safely managed drinking water, and pollution is linked to around nine million deaths a year.
Six of nine planetary boundaries are transgressed, and current policies point toward roughly 3 °C of warming.

The exposed majority is concentrated in Africa and South Asia: three to six-plus billion people could face one or more major stressors, and the two regions that contributed least to the damage hold the largest share of those exposed.
Crises amplify one another. Research on synchronous failure and crisis entanglement shows that shared drivers, feedbacks and common vulnerabilities turn separate problems into a single system risk.
Damage outlasts decisions: excess CO₂ persists for tens of thousands of years, ice sheets respond over millennia, and extinct species do not return on human timescales.

The extinction tail is real but uncertain. Expert estimates place the chance of existential catastrophe this century near one in six, and most of that risk comes from anthropogenic technologies — exactly the risks a degraded, conflict-prone world handles worst.

Long instability does not imply certain extinction. Extinction tens or hundreds of thousands of years out is a hypothetical terminal scenario, not a prediction; the framework’s value is showing how a civilization can remain vulnerable long after the initial catastrophe has passed.

The defining feature is the gap between survival and sustainable survival — humanity can persist, and prosper in places, while the underlying crisis is never resolved and the margin for survival narrows.
method: Every source is hyperlinked in the text and collected in Appendix B; Appendix C sets out methodology and limitations, and Appendix A is a glossary. Figures marked illustrative are conceptual and are not forecasts. The report examines the most pessimistic coherent version of the polycrisis story deliberately, as a framework rather than a prediction: the deep-time and terminal-extinction sections are hypothetical scenarios offered for analysis, and Section 14 is given over to counterarguments and uncertainty. This is the Global Risk & Earth Systems edition, a substantially rewritten successor to the earlier Polycrisis Apocalypse report (HH-2026-24, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23591850), with a different structure and framing rather than a corrected reprint.
